candidates.statement: The purpose of this guidance is to describe the nonclinical information that FDA recommends to 20 support an investigational new drug application (IND) for an antisense oligonucleotide being 21 developed to treat a severely debilitating or life-threatening (SDLT) disease caused by a unique 22 genetic variant where only a small number of individuals are prospectively identified (usually 23 one or two). The investigational antisense oligonucleotide should be from a well-characterized 24 chemical class 2 for which there is substantial nonclinical information and clinical experience that 25 is publicly available or to which the sponsor-investigator (hereafter referred to as sponsor) has a 26 right of reference. 27
candidates.context: This guidance is not intended to address nonclinical testing for commercial development of 29 oligonucleotides. 30

candidates.statement: Sponsors should include the following nonclinical safety studies in their IND submission: 56
candidates.context: III. IND-SUPPORTING SAFETY STUDIES 54 • Hybridization-dependent off-target assessment: Basic Local Alignment Search Tool 58 (BLAST) and other appropriate in silico and/or in vitro assessments of possible off-target 59 binding. 60

candidates.statement: • Safety pharmacology: For systemically administered investigational antisense 62 oligonucleotides, FDA recommends evaluating effects in the core safety pharmacology 63 battery—cardiovascular, central nervous, and respiratory systems. 4 These endpoints may 64 be assessed in the general toxicity study discussed below, if conducted in a rigorous 65 manner (ICH S7A). If a pharmacologically relevant species is available, sponsors should 66 use that species. 67

candidates.statement: 3 FDA regulations provide flexibility in applying regulatory standards because of the many types and intended uses of drugs. FDA “exercise[s] its scientific judgment” in determining the kind and quantity of data a sponsor is required to provide for individual drug development programs. See, for example, 21 CFR 314.105(c). This flexibility extends from the early stages of development to the design of adequate and well-controlled studies required to demonstrate effectiveness to support marketing approval and to establish safety data needed for the intended use. For further information on this topic, see the draft guidance for industry Rare Diseases: Common Issues in Drug Development (January 2019). When final, this guidance will represent the FDA’s current thinking on this topic. For the most recent version of a guidance, check the FDA guidance web page at https://www.fda.gov/regulatory-information/search-fda-guidance-documents .

candidates.statement: The primary goal of selecting the starting dose is to identify a dose that is expected to have 144 pharmacologic effects and is reasonably safe, and it should be scientifically justified based on the 145 totality of available data. 146
candidates.context: IV. FIH DOSE SELECTION 142 Sponsors should clearly describe and justify the method used for selecting the starting dose, 148 including the basis for calculating safety margins between doses tested in animals and the dose 149 or doses selected for administration in a human. For local administration, sponsors should take 150 into consideration organ weight, volume, or other measures as appropriate for interspecies dose 151 scaling. And for intrathecal administration, sponsors should calculate interspecies dose 152 comparisons based on a dose normalized to cerebrospinal fluid volume. 153

candidates.statement: When a steep dose-response or an exposure-response for severe toxicity is observed in 158 nonclinical toxicity studies, or when no preceding marker of severe toxicity is available, 159 sponsors should consider smaller than usual dose increments (e.g., fractional increments rather 160 than dose doubling) for clinical dosing. 161
candidates.context: For investigational antisense oligonucleotides within the scope of this guidance, the highest dose 163 or exposure assessed in the nonclinical studies does not necessarily limit the highest dose that 164 can be evaluated in humans, depending on the available nonclinical and clinical information and 165 the participant’s clinical situation. 166

candidates.statement: Expansion of this approach to other oligonucleotide chemistries or mechanisms of action (e.g., 184 siRNA), or to other treatment modalities (e.g., individualized biologics) should be supported by a 185 nonclinical approach that provides a similar understanding of the chemistry and mechanism of 186 action sufficient to allow for safe FIH dose selection, potential dose escalation, and an ability to 187 predict the likely adverse effects that could occur, and how these can be clinically monitored. 188 This will be considered by FDA on a case-by-case basis. 189
candidates.context: The nonclinical safety package described here differs from that generally recommended for non- 172 SDLT diseases, for treatment modalities other than antisense oligonucleotides, and for SDLT 173 diseases with larger patient populations. FDA considers the nonclinical safety package 174 recommended in this guidance acceptable to support INDs for investigational antisense 175 oligonucleotides within the scope of this guidance, in part because of existing experience with 176 antisense oligonucleotides and the ability to anticipate and manage some of the potential adverse 177 effects. However, the probability of identifying toxicity nonclinically may be reduced in 178 comparison to standard nonclinical safety testing, and the potential for clinically significant 179 adverse effects may therefore be increased.
